articles.title: 'Lost leverage across the board': Trump's strategy gets brutal update six months into war
articles.description: Six months after President Donald Trump launched the war in Iran on Feb. 28 — predicting it would last four to five weeks — the conflict has instead become a defining liability of his second term. Iranian forces have withstood months of bombardment, using mines and drones to keep degrading U.S. military capacity cheaply, and Trump's options are narrowed by his own-self imposed limits, reported the Washington Post . "Trump needs to reopen the Strait of Hormuz while operating within his own red lines: His fierce aversion to becoming a 21st-century Herbert Hoover, who presided over the Great Depression, limits the economic moves available to him," the Post reported. "His decision, at least so far, to hold back from the riskiest and most extreme military moves against Iran similarly limits his war options." Experts offered a harsh assessment of his strategy so far and questioned his decision to start the war in the first place. "We are in an absolutely weaker position, and I don't know that there's any redemption for it," said Suzanne Maloney of the Brookings Institution. Trump has pointed to a soaring stock market and insisted the Strait of Hormuz — a critical global oil corridor — remains open, saying Tehran can no longer pay its troops. But shipping data shows traffic through the strait has collapsed to as few as five vessels a day this week, down from more than 100 daily before the war, according to the tracking firm Kpler, even as U.S. officials say some ships are hiding their transponders. Oil prices have stayed elevated throughout. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week announced an "economic D-Day" of sanctions on countries doing business with Iran, then softened the threat by delaying enforcement so as not to "blow up the global financial system" — a hedge that sanctions expert Richard Nephew said signaled weakness to Tehran. “It clearly sent a signal to the Iranians that there is a limit to how far we’re going to be prepared to act,” said Nephew, who helped formulate the sanctions regime during the Obama administration before the 2015 Iran nuclear deal. “What worries me is whether or not we have now also, in addition, learned the limits to how far military coercion can push, and that actually the Iranian response is going to be, ‘We can handle all of this.’ In which case, it’s not just the the leverage on the economy that we’ve lost. We’ve lost leverage across the board,” Nephew added. Domestically, the war is dragging on Trump's approval , which a Reuters/Ipsos poll put at 33 percent this week, with support softening even among Republicans, though it remains 69 percent within his own party. U.S. intelligence assessments say Vladimir Putin now views Washington as weakened by the war and could be emboldened against Europe — prompting CIA Director John Ratcliffe's trip to Moscow this week to warn against further aggression toward Ukraine. Roughly a quarter of the U.S. Reaper drone fleet has been lost, and Patriot stockpiles are strained, leaving allies like Greece warier of arming Ukraine and pushing the Pentagon to weigh scaling back its Gulf presence. "We are not going to be the sole dominant presence in the Middle East in the way we were before," said Nate Swanson, a former National Security Council Iran director.

articles.title: White House 'not a happy place' right now amid Trump's 'frustrated mood': Maggie Haberman
articles.description: New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman revealed the mood inside the White House amid President Donald Trump's frustration. During a Thursday appearance on CNN, Haberman was asked about the White House environment as Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt wrapped up her final day. CNN anchor Laura Coates noted that the second Trump administration isn't seeing as much turnover as the first, but she expects "a lot of midterm anxiety" in the White House right now. "What's the morale like right now in the West Wing?" Coates asked Haberman. "A midterms [race], as you know, is often a time when people leave White Houses. These are grueling jobs. There are, you know, intensity times a thousand," Haberman explained, but she added that staffers are feeling more pressure than usual as Trump is in a bad mood. "It's not a happy environment by any of the reporting that we have," Haberman said. "The president has been in a pretty frustrated mood for a while about Iran, which, again, is of his own making." Haberman added that Trump "does not have the patience for long-term diplomacy or having these lengthy conversations to try to get out of a situation." Haberman and fellow New York Times reporter Jonathan Swan wrote Regime Change , which looks inside the White House during Trump's second administration. She told Coates that the book noted that Trump expected the conflict in Iran "to be a quick war." Trump expected that "this would be over fast, and that just is not how it worked out, and now there is a further depletion of munitions, and there are stories about that all the time," Haberman said. "And he is frustrated about leaks and on and on and on." As a result, "It's just not a happy environment" in the White House right now. "It is normal that people want to leave and want to go make money at this point, but it is very much not a happy place right now."

articles.title: US, South Korea and Japan to hold trilateral drill
articles.description: Seoul says South Korea, the U.S. and Japan will go ahead with a trilateral military drill next month to better deal with North Korean nuclear threats. South Korea’s military said in a statement Friday the annual Freedom Edge exercise will start on Sept. 7 for a five-day run in the waters off South Korea’s southern Jeju Island. The announcement comes a day after North Korea vowed to retaliate against what it called U.S. hostilities. The development further dims prospects for an early resumption of diplomacy between North Korea and the U.S., despite President Donald Trump’s recent decision to scale back a major bilateral military drill with South Korea.

articles.title: What are the main events for today?
articles.description: EUROPEAN SESSION In the European session, we don't have much on the agenda other than a couple of low-tier releases like the French PPI and ECB meeting minutes. The data won't change anything for the ECB, so the market reaction will be muted. As a reminder, the ECB is widely expected to hike interest rates by 25 bps in September, bringing the policy rate to 2.50%. This was also confirmed by "ECB sources" which reported that the central bank is ready to raise interest rates in September but added that there's little appetite to signal further tightening afterwards. AMERICAN SESSION In the American session, the only highlight is the US Jobless Claims figures. Initial Claims are expected at 208K vs 206K prior, while Continuing Claims are seen at 1790K vs 1799K prior. The US labour market has stabilised in recent weeks after a string of strong jobs data. Anyway, unless there are big deviations from expectations, the data is unlikely to be market-moving given the Fed's focus on inflation. CENTRAL BANK SPEAKERS 14:00 GMT/10:00 ET - Fed's Hammack (hawk - voter) This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.
